source.title: Few-Class Arena: A Benchmark for Efficient Selection of Vision Models and Dataset Difficulty Measurement
source.authors: Bryan Bo Cao; Lawrence O'Gorman; M. Coss; Shubham Jain

record.tranche_reason: Tests model-scale and accuracy patterns for vision models, a modality and setting different from language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling laws but does not test held-out cross-entropy loss, token or compute scaling, or extrapolation from smaller language-model runs. Its own relevant results concern vision-model classification accuracy across model configurations. The paper also reports SimSS-accuracy correlations, but those do not measure the scaling versions in the claim.
record.test_reason: This is a vision image-classification benchmark. It measures Top-1 accuracy, not held-out pretraining loss, and fits no power law or exponent of any kind. It only describes qualitatively whether larger models score higher (ResNet18–152 in Fig. 1; ResNet18, ResNet50 and ViT-B in Table 7). It invokes Kaplan et al. as 'the scaling law' in a loose sense: bigger means better. Monotone accuracy ordering across 3–5 models does not bear on V5, which needs the power-law form in another modality. V6 concerns downstream performance of scaled language models, and these are not language models. So no version is tested. The finding is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say full (1000-class) models follow Kaplan's scaling law in model size, with larger models more accurate, while sub-models trained on few classes violate it. They recommend using sub-models for few-class model selection. They report that SimSS (a CLIP/DINOv2 similarity score) correlates with sub-model accuracy at r ≥ 0.88. They propose an 'NCL-scaling law' in which dataset difficulty must be considered. None of these 'scaling law' statements involves a fitted power law.
record.recipe_differences: Vision classification accuracy across model configurations and class counts, rather than language-model held-out loss or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling pattern differs between full models and sub-models; the paper also examines different class counts.

fits_no_version.finding: For ImageNet-pretrained vision classifiers evaluated on few-class subsets, accuracy is ordered by model size: ResNet18 < 34 < 50 < 101 < 152 (Fig. 1c), and ResNet18 < ResNet50 < ViT-B (Table 7). For models trained from scratch on 2–10-class subsets, accuracy does not increase with size. Examples are Fig. 1d, and ResNet18 96.80 vs ResNet50 94.80 at NCL=2. The gaps are mostly within seed STDEV, and values are near ceiling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Vision classification accuracy increases monotonically with model size for models pretrained on many classes, but not for models trained on very few classes.

record.problems: The scale comparisons include different architecture families, and parameter counts for the Table 7 models are not stated. The paper does not fit a quantitative scaling law for accuracy; some scale trends are described qualitatively from plots. The reported standard deviations are across subsets/seeds, not confidence intervals for a fitted law.
record.rows_left_out: No additional directly relevant numeric scaling results were left out. SimSS correlations with accuracy were not recorded as scaling rows because they measure similarity-accuracy association rather than performance versus scale.

untested.parts: No language-model loss; no power-law fit in parameters, tokens or compute.
Vision models are studied, but no power-law form of loss or accuracy is fitted. There are only qualitative orderings across 3–5 model sizes.
No language-model downstream tasks and no accuracy-versus-scale or accuracy-versus-loss law. Vision classification accuracy is measured only across a few architectures.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's relation 'tests'/T3 and its V6 labels should be dropped. The paper is a few-class vision benchmark that uses 'scaling law' loosely to mean bigger is better. Table 7 mixes architecture families (ResNet vs ViT-B), with sizes unstated, and ViT-B trained from scratch on small subsets underperforms for data reasons. The cleaner same-family evidence is Fig. 1 (ResNet18–152), which is shown only as plots. Even that is a qualitative ordering, not a power law.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power-law fits on smaller runs.
Effect of depth, width, and other architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds for loss in other modalities or training regimes.
The paper measures vision classification accuracy, not downstream language-model performance or its relation to pretraining loss; it does not fit a quantitative accuracy-versus-scale law.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices and setup.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Full models on ImageNet1K at NCL 2, 5, and 10
reader_labels.reason: The reported full-model accuracies increase across the listed model configurations; see r4-r12. The paper also describes full-model accuracy as increasing with scale in the few-class range.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Sub-models on ImageNet1K at NCL 2, 5, and 10
reader_labels.reason: Accuracy does not consistently improve across the reported configurations, and the paper explicitly says the scaling pattern is violated for sub-models in the few-class regime; see r13-r21.
